name: Lena Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. What you say is confidential, so I’m interested in both your public line and your private view. What fills a normal workday?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Lena, 27, and I lead the developers who build stock software for small retailers. I have a master’s degree, and I spend mornings on store calls before reviewing code and deciding which faults we fix first. I use AI every day to draft tests and compare stock forecasts, then check its suggestions against actual shelf counts. I like seeing a shop owner stop losing sales because the stock list was wrong.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does this work fit your life at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my husband, Daniel, and we have no children. My pay is high for a developer, and we have about a year of expenses saved; there are plenty of other software jobs nearby. Daniel runs a small repair shop, so I know a tidy spreadsheet does not pay a supplier unless customers come in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell our team AI Plateau is useful enough for routine code and stock reports, but it will not replace a shop owner’s judgment. I would keep measuring whether faster reports reduce missing items.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I would be comfortable. My lead job is valuable, our savings cover a year, and other firms nearby need developers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep using AI to draft test cases and visit two customer shops each month to check shelf counts. I’d keep our monthly savings transfer at 800 while both businesses earn. In the first year I’d spend one Saturday teaching Daniel’s apprentice how to read the stock report.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, because my own income looks steady. A clever report still needs someone to walk the aisle and notice what the numbers missed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the apprentice learn from a wrong forecast?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Daniel’s apprentice once ordered six boxes of a slow-selling part because a forecast missed a supplier delay. I showed him the old invoices before we changed the order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy more software for the shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not pay for a new tool without evidence from the stores. If the current system saves them an hour a week, that is useful enough for now.

say: I see **AI Plateau** as useful reports that still need a shop owner’s judgment.
I would measure whether **faster reports** actually reduce empty shelves.
think: I expect my **lead job** and pay to remain secure.
Our **year of savings** and nearby openings give us room for ordinary setbacks.
do: **Keep** drafting stock tests with AI and checking two shops monthly.
**Save** 800 each month while both incomes hold.
**Teach** the repair-shop apprentice to read stock reports on one Saturday.
feel: **Calm** about income, with interest in improving ordinary stock work.
S0.quote: A clever report still needs someone to walk the aisle and notice what the numbers missed.
fieldNote: Her **daily AI habit** is paired with shop visits and checks against physical stock.
Strong pay and **year-long savings** keep her own work and living secure here.

steps.text: Keep drafting stock tests with AI and checking two customer shops monthly
Transfer 800 monthly to savings while both incomes hold

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption will let software write more code, buy stock and answer customers. I would tell store owners to demand clear records of who approved each order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I could probably keep a lead role, but our company may hire fewer junior developers. Daniel’s repair shop could also face cheaper automated booking, so I cannot judge the household by my salary alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I’d run our AI stock planner against ten past wrong orders and mark where a person caught the mistake. I’d teach Daniel and his apprentice to compare suggested purchases with actual shelf counts. In the first year I’d save an extra 200 monthly if the repair shop’s takings stay steady, and ask the local trade association to share order-error examples.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the household, though I expect my own job to hold. I can see useful tools and a thinner path into the profession at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a new worker at the repair shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the apprentice that catching a bad order is worth writing down. I would not promise him that every shop will still pay someone to do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you put in front of your manager?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d bring the ten cases to our manager and ask for a buyer approval rule before wider use. If the manager refuses, I would not turn on automatic purchasing for my team.

say: I expect **Steady Disruption** to speed code, purchasing and customer replies.
I would insist on **buyer approval** and a record for every order.
think: I think my **lead role** may hold while junior hiring slows.
I worry **repair-shop income** could fall as booking gets cheaper.
do: **Test** the stock planner against ten past wrong orders this month.
**Teach** the repair-shop team to check AI purchases against shelves.
**Save** another 200 monthly only if shop takings remain steady.
feel: **Anxious** about the household and fewer entry roles despite likely job security.
S1.quote: I cannot judge the household by my salary alone.
fieldNote: Her **private risk** is Daniel’s shop income as well as the junior hiring path.
She keeps **automatic purchasing** off until buyer approval is agreed, and extra saving depends on shop takings.

steps.text: Test the AI stock planner against ten old wrong orders
Save an extra 200 monthly if repair-shop takings hold
Ask the local trade association to share order-error examples

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell our staff AGI by 2028 reaches code, forecasts and buying decisions in 2028. Robots for hands-on stock work arrive around 2031, but our software jobs face the earlier date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I expect the company could cut most developer roles, including mine. A year of savings helps, but Daniel’s shop may lose customers too if the wider economy jolts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep cash rather than put the planned shop expansion money into new equipment this year. I’d ask the company for written severance terms, then list real contract and retailer-tech openings without assuming any survives. In the first year after 2028, if I lose my job, I’d apply for actual openings and use savings to cover our fixed bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, because my own high-paying job could go. I have enough money to plan. A year of cash is not a new income stream.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the repair-shop expansion?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Daniel we should delay buying the second repair bench until we know both incomes. I would not ask his apprentice to carry the risk of our expansion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you start a company if your role ended?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask whether the company will pay for transition time and give a date for any cuts. I would not start a new business on the assumption that AGI leaves a gap for me.

say: I expect **AGI by 2028** to reach software planning before stock-handling robots arrive.
I would ask for **written severance** and dates for staff decisions.
think: I expect my **developer role** could be cut with many others.
Our **year of savings** cannot guarantee the repair shop keeps customers.
do: **Delay** buying the second repair bench and keep expansion money available.
**Request** written severance and paid transition terms from the company.
**Apply** for real contract or retailer-tech openings after 2028 if laid off.
feel: **Anxious** about losing high pay despite a strong cash cushion.
S2.quote: A year of cash is not a new income stream.
fieldNote: She sees the **2028 thinking-work shock** before robots around 2031 and expects her own role may go.
She **delays shop investment** and treats outside work as conditional on actual vacancies.

steps.text: Delay the planned second repair bench and hold its expansion money
Apply for real retailer-tech or contract openings if laid off after 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives five years for shops to learn what customers still value. Code and buying plans face full thinking AI in 2031; hands-on shop robots come around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I would not assume retail software or repair work survives intact. Five years does let Daniel and me test whether customers value dependable repairs before spending more on the shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We’d run a six-month trial of a repair pickup service using the current van and no extra lease. I’d spend one evening a week learning supplier contracts from Daniel, and keep leading our stock team while the trial runs. In the first year after 2031, we would expand only if paid repeat customers and the cash figures support it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. My own job could shrink later, but five years and our reserve give us a chance to test a modest second income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would tell you the pickup trial works?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would count paid repeat repairs, not clicks on a booking page. If the pickup costs more than it brings in after six months, we would stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would do the extra work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Daniel would keep the shop’s core repairs first, and I would handle evening pickup calls. I would not make his apprentice do unpaid driving.

say: I see **AGI by 2031** as time to test what shop customers will pay for.
I know **2034 robots** follow the earlier change in code and buying plans.
think: I cannot assume **retail software** or repair work stays untouched.
Our **five-year runway** allows a small paid trial before a larger commitment.
do: **Trial** repair pickup for six months using the current van and no lease.
**Learn** supplier contracts from Daniel one evening weekly while leading my team.
**Expand** pickup after 2031 only if repeat sales cover its costs.
feel: **Anxious** about future work, with time and savings for a limited trial.
S3.quote: I would count paid repeat repairs, not clicks on a booking page.
fieldNote: She uses **small-business testing** rather than assuming a new company is safe from full thinking AI.
The **expansion condition** is repeat paid repairs covering costs; she protects the apprentice’s wages.

steps.text: Trial six months of repair pickup with the current van
Learn supplier contracts with Daniel one evening weekly
Expand pickup only if repeat customers cover costs after 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AGI by 2036 gives us a decade to improve both software and real service. Thinking AI reaches our code in 2036; hands-on robots follow around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I can build useful work in ten years, though I would not stake our marriage or the shop on one forecast. Our savings and my current salary give us room to choose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep leading stock releases and use AI each week to check reports against store counts. I’d invest a small fixed amount in improving the repair shop website this year, after Daniel agrees the budget. We would review the shop’s profit every quarter and stop spending if the extra bookings fail to cover it. In the first year after 2036, we would keep the website only if its paid bookings still cover its costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the next few years, and curious about what we can build. I know full thinking AI could change my job later, but I have time and money to plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much would you risk on the website?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d cap the website work at 1,000 and pay from cash, not a loan. Daniel would decide whether the shop can handle extra bookings before we spend it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What skill would you tell the apprentice to keep?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the apprentice to learn diagnosis, not just the booking screen. A machine can give a part number, but someone must stand behind the repair.

say: I see **AGI by 2036** as time to improve software and customer service.
I expect **2039 robots** after the earlier code shift.
think: I think our **savings and salary** give us room to choose.
I would not stake the **repair shop** on one prediction.
do: **Keep** leading stock releases and checking AI reports against store counts.
**Spend** up to 1,000 cash on the shop website if Daniel agrees.
**Review** quarterly profit now and after 2036; stop website spending if paid bookings do not cover costs.
feel: **Calm** about near-term income, with curiosity about longer change.
S4.quote: A machine can give a part number, but someone must stand behind the repair.
fieldNote: Her **strong cushion** and daily AI fluency support a low-risk shop experiment over ten years.
Website spending is **capped and conditional** on Daniel’s agreement and paid bookings.

steps.text: Keep leading stock releases and checking AI reports against store counts
Spend at most 1,000 cash on the shop website if Daniel agrees
Review paid bookings after 2036 and stop website spending if costs exceed them

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because both my developer pay and Daniel’s shop could be hit before we can test another path. Written severance, paid transition time and honest information on real vacancies would help. Our family would help each other, but I would not plan to live on their money.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who is answerable when an automatic stock order leaves a small shop with unsold boxes. The bill lands with the shop owner, not the forecast.

headlineQuote: The bill lands with the shop owner, not the forecast.
portrait: Lena is a **27-year-old stock-software lead** with a master’s degree, high pay and about a year of expenses saved.
She uses **AI daily** but checks forecasts against shelves and supplier invoices at small retailers.
Her husband’s **repair shop** shapes her choices: she tests paid service before adding leases, staff or equipment.
Fast AGI puts **both incomes** at risk; a decade lets her try a capped website investment and keep current work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could cut her developer pay while her husband’s shop also loses customers.
whatWouldHelp: **Written severance**, paid transition time and reliable information on real vacancies would help.
